uncited: Radial Opacity Change is an illustrative volume rendering technique that modulates voxel opacity based on the distance from a reference point (typically the object center or a user-defined focus point) to create a focus+context effect.

It solves the problem of visual clutter and occlusion during user interaction (rotation, panning, zooming) by making peripheral or distant structures more transparent, thereby revealing inner details.

It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly modeling opacity decay as a function of radial distance, inspired by the physics of viscous rotation, whereas [Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking](7928-spatial-importance-map-via-unsharp-masking.md) uses spatial frequency analysis and [Sparseness-based Color and Opacity Modulation](7932-sparseness-based-color-and-opacity-modulation.md) relies on local data density.
The method modifies the base opacity $\alpha_{base}$ of a voxel using an exponential decay function driven by a style function $S(t)$ and the Euclidean distance from the voxel to a reference center.
- Voxel position $\vec{P}_{voxel}$ in world or object space.
- Reference center position $\vec{P}_{center}$ (usually the geometric center of the volume).
- Base opacity $\alpha_{base}$ (optional, often incorporated into $S(t)$ or applied multiplicatively).
- Modulated opacity $\alpha_{voxel} \in [0, 1]$.
- No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard volume grid access.
The method is computed per-voxel or per-sample during ray casting.
Calculate the Euclidean distance $\rho$ between the current voxel position $\vec{P}_{voxel}$ and the reference center $\vec{P}_{center}$.
Compute the modulated opacity using the exponential decay formula.
In rotation scenarios, this is proportional to the angular velocity.
- **Precision:** If $S(t)$ is large and $\rho$ is large, the exponent becomes very negative, potentially underflowing to 0.
This is generally desired (opacity becomes 0), but ensure floating-point handling does not produce NaNs.
- **Boundary Conditions:** The formula assumes $\vec{P}_{center}$ is well-defined.
For non-convex or disconnected volumes, the geometric center may be outside the data, leading to unintuitive transparency gradients.

- **Zooming Logic:** The zooming formula $\max(0, \rho_{center} - \rho_{focus})$ implies that voxels closer to the focus point than the center will have 0 exponent (opacity 1) if $\rho_{focus} \ge \rho_{center}$.
It is distinct from the radial distance-based modulation of the parent method by using depth buffer values relative to the viewpoint.
- Voxels with high depth values (back side) are assigned high opacity to ensure visibility even if occluded by low depth voxels (front side).
- **Time Complexity:** $O(1)$ per voxel/sample, as it involves basic arithmetic operations (distance calculation, exponential).
It adds minimal overhead to the ray casting loop.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ auxiliary memory per voxel, as no additional large data structures are required.
The exponential function is the most expensive operation, but it is standard in graphics hardware.
It naturally reveals inner structures without complex preprocessing.
- **Limitations:** The "angular velocity" metaphor may not intuitively map to all types of user interactions (e.g., panning).
The choice of center point can be arbitrary for complex shapes.
- **When to use:** When the goal is to dynamically reveal internal structures during rotation or zooming in a volume visualization.
- **When not to use:** When precise quantitative analysis of outer structures is required, as they are intentionally made transparent.
It is inspired by the metaphor of a viscous fluid rotating around its center, where particles at the border have the highest speed and are candidates to disappear.
